conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the medicine team. I hear you came in with severe upper abdominal pain and vomiting. Can you tell me what’s been going on today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s this awful pain right in the middle, like burning and stabbing. I started throwing up and I can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Is the vomit bloody or does it look like coffee grounds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s not bloody. Just regular vomit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers, chills, chest pain, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Just nausea, pain, and I had diarrhea earlier this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How many times a day were you having diarrhea before you came in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bunch—several times a day. But today it’s mostly the vomiting and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you’ve had Roux-en-Y bypass in the past and then a reversal, and you’ve had ulcers before. Does this pain feel like those ulcer episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Exactly like that. And it gets worse when I try to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have you been taking your stomach medications—pantoprazole or ranitidine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stopped them. I felt like I didn’t need them anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful to know. In the emergency department you had a CT scan, and it did not show a bowel obstruction or a surgical complication. Surgery also evaluated you and didn’t think you needed an operation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt this much if the scan is normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A CT is good for blockages and major complications, but it can’t always show irritation of the stomach lining. Given your history and stopping acid medicines, one possibility is gastritis—irritation from acid or bile reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so nauseous I can’t swallow pills. And I need my Keppra—can I get it through the IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. For now we can give levetiracetam by IV while you’re too nauseated to take pills, and we’ll switch back to oral once you’re tolerating food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, your fingerstick blood sugar was around 70 when you arrived. That’s low-normal, and with poor intake it can make you feel shaky. We’ll give IV fluids with some dextrose and monitor your sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel shaky and weak. I’m scared it’s going to drop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep checking it. The goal is to support you until you can eat again, because eating small amounts regularly is usually what stabilizes it best for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The morphine helped a little in the ER. Can I keep getting that? My oxycodone at home didn’t touch this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We want to control pain, but IV opioids can worsen nausea, slow the gut, and can drop blood pressure. We’ll start with bowel rest, IV pantoprazole, and anti-nausea medicine, and we’ll reassess pain control frequently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just don’t want to suffer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll treat the underlying irritation and use safer pain options as much as possible—acetaminophen and, if needed, tramadol by mouth once you can tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: any more vomiting since you got to the floor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not since the last Zofran, but I still feel queasy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll keep Zofran available as needed and keep you NPO for now—just letting your stomach rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Overnight was quiet. How’s the pain and nausea right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still hurts in the same spot. Nausea is a little better, but I’m afraid to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. GI is going to see you today. Our working thought is bile reflux or gastritis related to your post-surgical anatomy and stopping the reflux meds. We’re continuing IV pantoprazole twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are they going to do an endoscopy now? I feel like that’s the only way to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll ask them directly. Sometimes, if symptoms improve with bowel rest and stronger acid suppression, they recommend deferring endoscopy to outpatient—especially if there’s no bleeding and the CT is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI evaluated you. They think this fits bile reflux gastritis. Their recommendation is bowel rest, IV PPI, then slowly advance your diet, and focus on smaller, more frequent meals to reduce reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no EGD while I’m here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. They feel an inpatient EGD is unlikely to change what we do today, because the main treatment is exactly what we’re already doing—high-dose PPI and protecting the stomach lining. You also have an outpatient plan with your gastroenterologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m frustrated. This keeps happening and no one fixes it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. What we can do in the hospital is make sure there’s no emergency problem, get symptoms under control, and set you up with the right follow-up testing and long-term plan. We’ll also add sucralfate to coat the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood pressure feels low. I’m dizzy when I sit up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is on the low side, and you’ve had low readings before. We’re giving IV fluids now. Also, opioids like morphine can worsen low blood pressure, so we’re going to stop IV morphine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If you stop it, what am I supposed to take for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use acetaminophen and, once you can take pills, tramadol as needed. We’ll also keep treating the stomach irritation—often that’s what drives the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you doing with sips of clear liquids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can sip a little. It still burns, but I’m not throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep it slow and see if we can advance to small, bland meals tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Any diarrhea since you’ve been here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, actually. I haven’t really gone much at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given that, we’re not going to send stool tests right now. You mentioned you stopped the vancomycin taper because you ran out—since you’re not having significant diarrhea in the hospital, we’re not treating C. diff during this stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it still be C. diff even without diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: C. diff typically causes frequent watery diarrhea. Without that, it’s less likely to be the driver of your current symptoms. We’ll keep watching, and if diarrhea returns we can reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugars have been stable since you started taking in some calories. We’re going to stop the dextrose-containing IV fluids and continue checking fingersticks for a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the shaky feeling was from not eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s our best explanation. We didn’t see dangerously low values on blood tests, but low-normal sugars can still make you feel unwell, especially with your history after bariatric surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I switch back to my Keppra pills? The IV keeps beeping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you’re keeping liquids down, yes—we can transition back to oral levetiracetam today and stop the IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I saw you walking in the hallway earlier. How’s the nausea and pain with the small meals?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can eat a little at a time. If I eat too much, it feels like it comes right back up. The pain is still there, but not as sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That pattern fits bile reflux. The plan is small, frequent meals and staying on pantoprazole twice a day. We’re also continuing ranitidine and sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe to take all of those together?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but timing matters. Sucralfate can interfere with absorption of other meds, so we’ll give you a schedule—usually sucralfate four times a day, spaced away from other pills when possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried you’re sending me home without figuring it out. I want an EGD before I leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear the concern. We spoke again with the GI team. They still feel an inpatient EGD won’t change the immediate treatment and that you’re better served keeping your planned outpatient endoscopy with your gastroenterologist, where they can follow results and adjust long-term management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But what if it’s an ulcer again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it is an ulcer, the first-line treatment is high-dose acid suppression and protecting the lining—exactly what we’re doing. The key is staying on the meds consistently and following up for the scope. If you develop black stools, vomiting blood, fainting, or worsening severe pain, you should come back immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For pain control, we’re avoiding oxycodone and other stronger narcotics here because of the low blood pressure and nausea. How is tramadol working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It helps some. Not perfect, but I can manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You finished breakfast?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I ate a small tray. No vomiting. Still tender, but it’s like my usual pain now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Your vitals look stable. We’ll discharge you today with pantoprazole twice daily, ranitidine, and sucralfate, plus Zofran as needed. For pain: acetaminophen and tramadol as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to do anything special with meals at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—small, frequent meals, and avoid large portions that trigger reflux. Keep taking the reflux medications even if you feel better. And keep your GI follow-up for the outpatient endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my low blood sugar episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The best prevention is regular small meals and not going long stretches without eating. If you feel shaky, check your sugar if you can and take quick carbohydrates, then follow with a small snack. Come in if you can’t keep anything down again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m still upset, but I can go if the plan is solid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fair. We’ll print your medication list and the warning signs to watch for. We’ll also make sure you have the GI appointment information before you leave.
